summary:
We created an interactive website, Lost in Space, to help users explore the stories and ongoing science behind gear dropped or left behind in Low Earth Orbit, on the Moon, and on Mars. 

Most people write off abandoned space gear as useless "space junk." We built Lost in Space to show how forgotten or dropped items often turn into accidental scientific tools - acting as "in-field weather reporters" on Mars, bouncing lasers from the Moon for over 50 years, or helping scientists model atmospheric re-entry.

We aim to inspire people and hare the message that even "space junk" can help make worthy contributions to science.
details:
We created an interactive website, Lost in Space, to help users explore the stories and ongoing science behind gear dropped or left behind in Low Earth Orbit, on the Moon, and on Mars.

Most people write off abandoned space gear as useless "space junk." We built Lost in Space to show how forgotten or dropped items often turn into accidental scientific tools - acting as "in-field weather reporters" on Mars, bouncing lasers from the Moon for over 50 years, or helping scientists model atmospheric re-entry.

We aim to inspire people and hare the message that even "space junk" can help make worthy contributions to science.

Project Description

Lost in Space is an interactive, scroll-driven web experience exploring the stories and ongoing science behind gear dropped or left behind in Low Earth Orbit, on the Moon, and on Mars. As you scroll through three cosmic zones, you can inspect seven custom-illustrated artifacts—from Ed White’s Gemini 4 glove to Apollo lunar mirrors and Perseverance’s thermal foil. Clicking any card opens a four-chapter story drawer alongside mission telemetry, an archival NASA photo reveal, and direct source links, while a Mission Explorer tracker (0/7 to 7/7) logs your discoveries.

Benefits and Goals

Accessible Science: Turns dense mission logs and orbital data into an engaging, easy-to-follow visual journey.

Smooth Performance:  Uses lightweight vector art on the main scroll and only loads high-res NASA photos when a card is clicked, keeping the site fast and lag-free.

Verifiable Data: Links every artifact directly to official NASA open-data archives so anyone can check the primary sources.

Tech Stack

Prototyping & Frontend: Base44, React, TypeScript/JavaScript, HTML5, and custom CSS3 (using GPU-accelerated transforms, scroll-snap, and responsive grids), plus `zod` (v4.6.7) for schema validation.

Hardware: Standard team laptops for research, writing, UI testing, and CSS debugging.

Innovation Highlights

Atmosphere & Storytelling: Designed like an interactive mission dossier rather than a dry textbook, pairing minimalist vector art with a "click-to-reveal" photo mechanic.

Performance-First CSS:  Separated initial vector graphics from modal photography and fine-tuned custom CSS properties (`will-change`, scroll-snap) for butter-smooth scrolling.

Curated Focus: Handpicked seven standout artifacts across Orbit, the Moon, and Mars that best show real, ongoing scientific value.

Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

 Used Base44 for app scaffolding and AI tools for brainstorming and refining copy. All code, data, and text were reviewed, edited, and verified by our team.
